Pe Pământ „ora” amestecă trei lucruri: <: On Earth, “time” mixes three things: how fast a clock runs, where the Sun is in the sky and how far away the other party is. On other worlds these three things come apart. The ORARIUM method treats them separately and recombines them with two formulas valid for any body, from Mercury to a comet.
Secunda SI, aceeași peste tot. Fiecare c: The SI second, the same everywhere. Each body gets a Local Surface Time (LST): the proper time of an atomic clock on its reference equipotential surface, the analogue of Earth’s TT. On average, LST differs from UTC by a calculable rate ρ, to which are added small periodic terms and an origin set by convention. For the Moon, ρ ≈ 56 µs/day is the figure from the article. The official scale discussed there (“coordinated lunar time”) is a related coordinate scale, with its rate and origin fixed by convention; ORARIUM uses the proper time of the surface.
Ziua solară locală se împarte în <b>24 o: The local solar day is divided into 24 local hours × 60 min × 60 local s. The local hour lasts Psol/24 SI seconds, so noon is at 12:00 on every world. The body’s clock is left untouched; only the numbering of the day adapts. A year is expressed in local days.
Care e <i>ora</i>, nu doar ritmul? Faza: What is the time, not just the rhythm? The phase can come from the IAU orientation + ephemeris (planets), from the mean elongation (Moon), from MTC (Mars); for synchronous satellites, asteroids and dwarf planets without an IAU orientation in the app, for now only the rhythm is available. Their orbital phase requires dedicated ephemerides; until then the rhythm remains correct, and the time is anchored to the first mission.
Lumina are nevoie de minute sau ore. Ori: Light takes minutes or hours. Every message carries the triplet (LST, UTC, ρ); the receiver subtracts the light time and applies ρ, thus reconstructing the event without negotiation. For Mars, a signal takes between ≈3 and ≈22 minutes.

<b>Cine decide?</b> Conferința Generală: Who decides? The General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM, 28th, Versailles) adopted, according to the article, a resolution aimed at defining an international reference scale for lunar time; the concrete choice of scale remains open. ORARIUM proposes the general form: the same mechanism, applied to each body.
<b>Altitudine zero?</b> Nu „nivelul mări: Zero altitude? Not “sea level”, but the mean equipotential surface (generalised geoid: selenoid, areoid), defined by the potential W0. Each metre of altitude adds g·h/c² (see the calculator in each body’s sheet).
<b>Rețea de ceasuri?</b> Propunerea ORAR: A network of clocks? The ORARIUM proposal: an ensemble (≥3 atomic clocks on the ground + relays in orbit) with a weighted average, like UTC, which produces LST. Each body with a human presence gets its own ensemble.
<b>Sincronizare?</b> Propunerea ORARIUM,: Synchronisation? The ORARIUM proposal, through the Bridge Clock: (LST, UTC, ρ) in every packet, plus light time (one-way and round trip) from the ephemeris.
Calculul e de ordinul întâi (Soare + pla: The calculation is first-order (Sun + parent planet + surface + rotation, orbits circular on average). For Mars it gives ≈488 µs/day, while the full models in the literature give ≈477 µs/day, with periodic variations of hundreds of µs due to eccentricity. The “real” times use mean IAU orientations (without librations) and simplified Keplerian ephemerides: the order of magnitude of the error is minutes (checked on Mars against the Mars24 formula, maximum deviation ≈4 min), not seconds. The light time is exact to ≈0.5%. TT = UTC + 69.184 s assumes that no further leap seconds have been introduced after 2017. For real navigation, full numerical ephemerides are used.

The ranking is an indicative index, not an official scientific assessment: it combines seven measurable factors with your weightings. A very weak factor drags the whole index down, because a habitat cannot make up for the lack of one vital thing with an excess of another.
